outline: Infectious and immunologic, including microbiologic and host response to insult
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Cat-scratch disease due to Bartonella henselae presenting with regional lymphadenitis
mechanism: Bartonella henselae can be transmitted after a cat scratch, particularly from a kitten. Typical cat-scratch disease causes a papule or pustule at the inoculation site followed by enlarged, tender regional lymph nodes and often a low-grade fever.
vignette: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of a painful swelling in her right axilla and low-grade fever. Three weeks ago, her family adopted a kitten. While she was playing with it, one of its claws broke the skin on the dorsum of her right hand. The kitten remains well and has no visible skin lesions. A small papule developed at the injury site and is still visible. Examination shows a tender 3-cm right axillary lymph node. There is no pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Infectious mononucleosis can cause fever and lymphadenopathy, but it more typically produces prominent fatigue, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy involving the neck and sometimes axillae; hepatosplenomegaly can also occur. The inoculation papule followed by ipsilateral regional lymphadenitis after a kitten scratch points instead to cat-scratch disease.

Toxoplasmosis may cause a flu-like illness with swollen lymph nodes, but human infection is commonly acquired through contaminated food or accidental ingestion of material contaminated by cat feces rather than by a scratch followed by a local papule and draining-node lymphadenitis.

Ulceroglandular tularemia can cause regional lymphadenopathy after inoculation, but CDC describes a skin ulcer at the entry site and typical exposure through tick or deer-fly bites or handling infected animals. The resolving papule after a kitten scratch and low-grade fever are more characteristic of cat-scratch disease.

Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis can follow traumatic inoculation and begins with a painless cutaneous bump, but additional bumps may develop, enlarge, ulcerate, and spread proximally along the affected limb. This patient instead has the characteristic cat-scratch disease pattern of an inoculation papule with tender regional lymphadenitis.
key_expl: This patient has cat-scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae. The key sequence is a kitten scratch followed by a papule at the inoculation site and then tender ipsilateral regional lymphadenopathy with low-grade fever. CDC identifies this combination as typical of cat-scratch disease, and the official USMLE 2026 content outline explicitly lists cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) among primary infections of lymphoid tissue.
objective: Recognize cat-scratch disease as the most likely diagnosis when a child develops a papule at a kitten-scratch site followed within several weeks by low-grade fever and tender regional lymphadenopathy.
clues: child with recent kitten claw inoculation
absence of pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly

sources.support: Supports B. henselae as the cause, usual acquisition after skin-breaking cat exposure especially from kittens, the fact that many infected cats are not ill, low-grade fever, tender lymph nodes 1–3 weeks after cat exposure, and a papule or pustule at the inoculation site.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Infectious Mononucleosis (Mono)
sources.support: Supports the mononucleosis distractor distinction: extreme fatigue, fever, sore throat, neck/axillary lymphadenopathy, and possible hepatosplenomegaly.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: About Toxoplasmosis
sources.support: Supports the toxoplasmosis distractor distinction: often asymptomatic in immunocompetent people, possible flu-like illness with swollen lymph nodes, and transmission through contaminated food or accidental ingestion after contact with cat feces/contaminated soil.

sources.support: Supports the sporotrichosis distractor distinction: cutaneous infection begins as a usually painless bump and can progress to additional enlarging lesions that suppurate, ulcerate, and spread up an extremity; cat-associated transmission occurs, particularly in areas where infected cats transmit disease, and CDC advises avoiding cats with sores or wounds.
